items.claim: One of the grounds on which the row refuses the interior seam at Ezek.33.6/Ezek.33.7 is not true on the bytes. Ezek.33.7 carries the 'and you, son of man' command opening, which turns the watchman figure onto the prophet himself; that is the same device this cluster accepts as a row onset at Ezek.33.10 and again at Ezek.33.30, so it is not the case that Ezek.33.7 offers no fresh onset. The decision to hold Ezek.33.1-Ezek.33.9 whole is nevertheless right, and the row's other two grounds carry it.
items.both_sides: Onset side at Ezek.33.7: the 'and you, son of man' command opening, with the watchman charge now laid on the prophet. Close side at Ezek.33.6: a closed-section mark and nothing else, because no recognition refrain and no utterance signature stands anywhere in Ezek.33.1-Ezek.33.9 (0 of those 9 verses carries either), and a paragraph mark never cuts on its own. The size guard bars the split as well: Ezek.33.7-Ezek.33.9 would be a three-verse remainder and it is not a complete word-event unit. Behind the row's own onset, Ezek.33.1 is a strict-form word-event and a hard seam with an open-section mark after MT 32:32 in front of it, and the address returns from the nations to the children of your people at Ezek.33.2. The seam at Ezek.33.7 therefore fails on its close side, not for want of an onset device.

items.claim: Two facts. First, the row's close argument over-extends a verbatim claim: the quoted complaint that the Lord's way is not fair does stand at both Ezek.33.17 and Ezek.33.20, but the judgment clause the row quotes alongside it stands only at Ezek.33.20, and the verb introducing the complaint differs in person between the two verses, so what repeats is the quoted saying and not the verdict. Second, the row refuses the interior seam at Ezek.33.11/Ezek.33.12 on a rule that does not reach it: it invokes the rule that an oath opening never becomes a row onset, but under the alternative the row itself frames, the onset would be the 'and you, son of man' command at Ezek.33.12, while the oath sits at Ezek.33.11 on the close side.
items.both_sides: Close side at Ezek.33.11: an open-section mark follows MT 33:11, but the signature in that verse is attached to the oath near the verse opening and the verse ends on a question put to the house of Israel, so it is not a verse-final oracle signature. This cluster already draws that distinction correctly elsewhere, classing the oath-attached signature at Ezek.34.8 as internal against the verse-final signatures at Ezek.34.15, Ezek.34.30 and Ezek.34.31. Onset side at Ezek.33.12: the 'and you, son of man' command plus a turn of address from the house of Israel to the children of your people. That pairing is at least as strong as the seam the row's own onset rests on at Ezek.33.9/Ezek.33.10, where the close side offers a closed-section mark and no signature at all, so the row's stated ground does not separate the two sites. What actually holds this span whole is the size guard, since a cut at Ezek.33.12 leaves Ezek.33.10-Ezek.33.11 as a two-verse remainder that is not a complete word-event unit, reinforced by the house-of-Israel address that opens Ezek.33.10 and closes Ezek.33.20. The eleven-verse span stands and medium_low is the right level for a span carrying a live interior candidate. Separately, the word-event that frames this span stands at Ezek.33.1 and the row records it nowhere.

items.claim: The row's own notes deny that it has a tier-1 onset, while its onset at Ezek.33.21 is a year-bearing dateline, one of the book's fourteen, ranked tier-1 in the frame spine and described in the device census as the strongest onset evidence the book offers. The denial also contradicts the same sentence's first clause, which names that dateline as one of the two things bounding the span. The two-verse size is forced by a hard seam on each side, not conceded for want of onset evidence.
items.both_sides: Onset side: the year-bearing dateline at Ezek.33.21, a hard seam, with an open-section mark after MT 33:20 behind it. Close side: an open-section mark after MT 33:22 and then the fresh strict-form word-event at Ezek.33.23, itself a hard seam, so the span cannot run forward into the next unit; and because Ezek.33.21 is a hard seam in its own right, it cannot run backward either. The span is therefore the only one available. The two verses are further welded to each other by the pair of events the book anticipates together, the arrival of the one who escapes at Ezek.24.26 and the mouth opened and no longer mute at Ezek.24.27, against the muteness laid on the prophet at Ezek.3.26; the row asserts that anticipation without its verse anchor. The hand-of-YHWH reading at Ezek.33.22 is correctly handled: it is 1 of the 7 construct matches, and the row is right that it opens no vision here.

items.both_sides: Onset side at Ezek.34.17: the messenger formula with the address turning to the flock directly in the second-person feminine plural, distinct from the shepherds who are spoken of in the third person across Ezek.34.1-Ezek.34.16; the form claim is exact on the bytes and the cut is licensed. Close side at Ezek.34.16: the promise completed with no formula and no mark, standing behind the verse-final signature at Ezek.34.15. Forward, the span closes at Ezek.34.31 on a verse-final signature with an open-section mark after it, immediately before the fresh strict-form word-event at Ezek.35.1. Two interior alternatives were weighed and both fail. At Ezek.34.19/Ezek.34.20 a closed-section mark follows MT 34:19 and a messenger formula opens Ezek.34.20, but the address does not durably change, because Ezek.34.21 returns to second-person plural verbs charged against the flock, so the third-person phrase at Ezek.34.20 frames a speech still aimed at the same hearers; and Ezek.34.19 carries no signature, leaving a mark alone on the close side. At Ezek.34.24/Ezek.34.25 the emphatic close at Ezek.34.24 is real but no onset device follows at Ezek.34.25. The fifteen-verse span therefore stands whole, and the row is right that the refrains at Ezek.34.27 and Ezek.34.30 are paragraph-final because Ezek.34.31 restates the covenant formula after them with a signature of its own.

triage_answers.decision: Not in my cluster. P04-008 sits in p04, I did not read it or the verses around it, and I decide neither its seam nor its confidence. I answer only the one part of the entry that reaches into c16, the condition it attributes to P08-002. As P08-002 actually states that condition, a sub-onset counts as a row seam only where a refrain-grade close stands immediately before it, and P08-002 itself classes the signature at Ezek.33.11 as internal rather than refrain-grade because it is attached to the oath near the verse opening and is not verse-final. The entry's own bytes show the signature at MT 21:18 standing at the end of the verse, which is the opposite case, so the condition as stated at P08-002 does not exclude that site. Whether the seam should be cut, and whether high survives, still turns on the p04 bytes and on whatever continuity that row argues, which I have not read.
triage_answers.both_sides: Stated only for the part that falls in my cluster. Inside c16 the operative distinction is verse-final against oath-attached: the signatures at Ezek.34.15, Ezek.34.30 and Ezek.34.31 stand at the end of their verses and are treated as refrain-grade, while those at Ezek.33.11 and Ezek.34.8 are attached to the oath near the verse opening and both rows treat them as internal. That distinction is applied consistently across my seven rows and it is the one the entry's 'for a seam' bullet depends on. Weighing the MT 21:18/21:19 seam itself, and the sword figure the row may argue across it, needs the p04 rows and their neighbours, which are outside my cluster; I take no position.

unresolved_uncertainty.what: Whether the 'and you, son of man' command opening is meant to count as a row onset in its own right or only as a sub-onset inside a word-event unit. The frame spine calls the son-of-man address onset corroboration and never an onset alone, while the granularity rule lists that command among the onsets a row may be cut at. MT ch 33 carries four of them, at Ezek.33.7, Ezek.33.10, Ezek.33.12 and Ezek.33.30, and this cluster cuts at two and not at the other two.
unresolved_uncertainty.why_it_matters: On the bytes it is the close side and the size guard, not the device, that separate the four sites, yet three of my rows argue from the device as though it were decisive. If the device is read as decisive, two more cuts look licensed here and neither should be taken.

unresolved_uncertainty.what: Whether the interior site at Ezek.34.19/Ezek.34.20 should be recorded in P08-015 as a weighed alternative rather than only as internal texture. I judge that it fails, because the address does not durably change across Ezek.34.20 and Ezek.34.21, but the row never weighs it and its rejected alternative looks only at the merge with the preceding span.
unresolved_uncertainty.why_it_matters: The row itself concedes fifteen verses sits above the target band, so its one interior site carrying both a paragraph mark and a messenger formula is the first thing a later reader will test, and the answer is not recorded anywhere in the row.

unresolved_uncertainty.what: Where a paragraph mark stands inside its verse. The inventory records only which verse a mark follows, so for every close in this cluster that rests on a mark I could confirm the verse and not the position.
unresolved_uncertainty.why_it_matters: At Ezek.33.11, the one verse in this cluster where a mark sits beside a signature that is not verse-final, the mark's position would settle whether the open section begins at Ezek.33.12 or inside Ezek.33.11, which is exactly the interior question I left as a keep.

unresolved_uncertainty.what: Whether the two-verse span at Ezek.33.21-Ezek.33.22 is inside or outside the over-split guard. The guard admits a row under three verses only where it is a complete word-event unit, and this span is not one, since its onset is a dateline rather than a word-event; the guard then names this very span as held, so the exception is recorded but its ground is not.
unresolved_uncertainty.why_it_matters: On my reading the span is forced by hard seams on both sides and needs no exception at all, but a later lane applying the guard literally could reopen a row whose boundaries are among the best evidenced in the cluster.

e19_selfreport: I ran no listing, no glob and no recursive search, my own scratch included. Every file I opened was named in my brief, in my launch message, in the governance set my own global policy requires, or was the ledger my launch message named, and each was opened by its exact path. My only self-checks were per-file SHA-256 digests taken by exact path; I tested no directory for existence. My private working copy went into a uniquely named subdirectory of my own session scratchpad, created without an existence check, and I wrote nothing under the worktree, touched no registry and wrote no receipt.
